newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's dollar to rise on firm fiscal footing.
newsitem.headline: Canada's dollar to rise on firm fiscal footing.

text.p: Canada's dollar is expected to rise, perhaps by as much as six U.S cents by the end of 1997, boosted by the federal government's tight fiscal policy.
Most of the 20 economists polled in a Reuter survey predicted the Canadian dollar would strengthen over the next two years.

One economist told the survey the Canadian dollar would rise by up to six cents from its current level around US$0.74. Another economist said the currency would weaken by up to three cents. The average prediction was for a one-cent rise.
Canada's dollar is benefitting from a decline in its foreign borrowing requirement. In August, Canada recorded its first quarterly current account surplus in 12 years.

"In other words, we don't need foreigners to buy our bonds anymore," said Michael Gregory, economist and senior strategist at Lehman Brothers in Toronto. "All we need to do is have them keep rolling over the ones they have."
Canada posted a C$1.15 billion surplus in its second-quarter net transactions with the rest of the world, compared with a C$1.62 billion deficit in the first quarter.
The surplus is the result of a program of fiscal restraint and deficit reduction initiated by Canada's Liberal government after it was elected in 1993.
"I think right now it is the competitiveness policies that government has put in over the last little while have created the current account surplus," Lehman's Gregory said.

The currency is expected to strengthen on what some economists have been calling a "virtuous cycle" where the improving current account makes it easier for the government to keep cutting its budget deficit, letting it drop interest rates, reducing debt service costs and thus foreign borrowing.

Last week, Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said the federal government was clearly on track to a balanced budget, although he did not specify a date. He projected a 1998/99 deficit of C$9 billion (US$6.6 billion) versus a 1996/97 deficit target of C$24.3 billion (US$17.96 billion).
"There are a number of factors that will contribute to a stronger Canadian dollar," said Douglas Porter, an economist at Nesbitt Burns."
He said monetary policy, which has been weighted heavily toward lower interest rates, would be rejigged in early 1997 to let the currency strengthen without an immediate cut in interest rates.
"I think going into 1997 we're going to see a stabilization of Bank (of Canada) policy."

That means the Bank of Canada will not be as likely to cut short-term interest rates each time the Canadian dollar strengthens, preferring instead to tighten monetary policy by letting a stronger Canadian dollar dry up some of the marginal demand in the export sector.
